name: Elena Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Elena. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Whatever you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a claims clerk at a small mutual insurer, which means it's owned by its members, not by shareholders. We cover homes and contents for about forty thousand households in our area. My day is mostly burst pipes, break-ins and storm damage. I open the claim, check the policy wording, arrange the loss adjuster if it's a big one, and write to the member about what's covered.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the phone calls, believe it or not. An older lady rings because her ceiling has come down, and you can hear she's frightened, and by the end she's calmer because someone has taken charge. What wears me down is the new online portal. Members get stuck on it and then ring me cross, and I'm not a computer person either.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about life outside work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27, and I'm engaged to Marco, who's an electrician. We're getting married next September at the church where my parents married, so most of our savings, about three months' worth, is spoken for. I have a two-year college diploma in office administration. I've been at the mutual six years. I don't use any of those AI chat programs, and I don't plan to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I'm glad people came to their senses. At work I'd say it to Margaret, my supervisor, over tea, because she's no fan of it either. I'm not online much, apart from the church group chat, and I wouldn't bring it up there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved. But I don't think it means nothing changes for me. The mutual already wants members to claim online, and even small bits of automation could take the letter-writing off me, which is a good third of my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep my head down. We'd keep putting money aside for the wedding, about 400 a month, and I'd keep my overtime on Saturdays during storm season. I'd avoid volunteering for anything to do with the portal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, with a little knot still there. There's always something with money when you're planning a wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the letter-writing could go. What would that mean for your hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a third of my day goes, then either they give me more claims or they ask whether they need four of us in the household team. Margaret's been there twenty-two years, so it wouldn't be her. It would be one of the younger ones, and I'm one of the younger ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money pressure, separate from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding, and after that a house. Marco and I rent a flat above a bakery, and prices round here have gone up and up. Even if AI does nothing, I'm working Saturdays just to stand still.

say: I'd say I'm **glad** people came to their senses about AI.
I'd mention it to my **supervisor** Margaret over tea, but not online or at church.
think: I'd feel **relieved**, but the mutual still pushes members to claim **online**.
Small automation could still take the **letter-writing**, about a third of my day.
do: Carry on and **keep my head down**, avoiding anything to do with the portal.
Keep saving about **400 a month** for the wedding next September.
Keep my **Saturday overtime** during storm season.
feel: Mostly **relieved**, with a small knot of worry about **money**.
S0.quote: Even if AI does nothing, I'm working Saturdays just to stand still.
fieldNote: Her pressures predate AI: a **wedding**, rising rent and Saturday overtime.
She sees even small automation threatening the **letter-writing** third of her day.
She notes the **youngest clerks** would go first, and counts herself among them.

steps.text: Keep handling household claims and avoid portal projects
Save 400 a month toward the September church wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same questions for the next one. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, and that people still want to talk to a real person when their kitchen is flooded. At work I'd say the mutual should remember what it's for. That's what I'd say to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be one of the first to go. Answering members and writing letters is exactly what's on that list. And I'm the one in the household team who refuses to touch the new tools, so I'm not exactly making it hard for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still not learn the AI tools, if I'm honest. I'd ask Margaret straight out whether my job is safe, and I'd keep my eyes open for jobs at the two other insurers in town, in case. Marco and I would cut the wedding guest list from 120 to about 80 to keep more money back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd feel like the world had decided to leave me behind and nobody asked me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said refusing the tools makes you easier to cut. Why not learn them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust them, and I don't want to train the thing that replaces me. My dad was a printer, and when the machines came in he worked harder and kept his head up, and it still didn't save him. I'd rather be good at the part people still need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to if your job did go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first. Marco's dad has a small electrical business and his mum does the books, and she's getting tired of it. And our church has people who look out for each other. I wouldn't go to the government unless there was nothing else.

say: I'd say people still want a **real person** when their kitchen floods.
I'd tell colleagues the mutual should **remember** it's owned by its members.
think: I'd be one of the **first to go**, since answering members and letters are listed.
Refusing the new tools makes me **easier to cut**, and I know it.
do: Ask my supervisor **straight out** whether my job is safe.
Watch for openings at the **two other insurers** in town.
Cut the wedding guest list from **120 to 80**.
feel: **Anxious**, like the world decided to **leave me behind** without asking.
S1.quote: My dad was a printer, and when the machines came in he worked harder and kept his head up, and it still didn't save him.
fieldNote: She knowingly **refuses the tools** and sees it raising her risk, but won't budge.
Her father's experience as a **printer** shapes her distrust.
Her fallback is **family and church**, with government help a last resort.

steps.text: Ask her supervisor Margaret whether the household claims job is safe
Check vacancies at the two other insurers in town
Cut the wedding guest list from 120 to 80

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is the fastest. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I don't believe it until I see it. And if it did happen, I'd say it's the wrong way to treat people, putting machines first. At church I'd say we'll need each other more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me. If a machine can do almost any thinking work by 2028, then my desk is just gone. My whole job is reading wording and talking to members, and there's nothing hands-on about it at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think we'd move the wedding forward, have it small, and put the rest toward keeping the flat. I'd ask Marco's mum if I could take over the books at the electrical business, since that's family. And I'd start asking at the care home where my aunt works, because looking after people is hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sums?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether Marco's wage covers the rent on its own. It just about does, if we stop eating out and drop the car. Our savings would last maybe three months, and after that, if I lost my job, I'd be relying on my fiancé Marco, which isn't how I wanted to start a marriage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the books at Marco's family business. Isn't that thinking work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, you're right, and I hadn't thought of that. A machine would do the books too, wouldn't it? So really it's the care home. The robots come later in this picture, about 2031, and being with old people is something I'd actually be good at.

say: I'd say I won't **believe it** until I see it.
I'd say putting **machines first** is the wrong way to treat people, and we'd need each other.
think: It **frightens** me, because my desk job would simply be gone by 2028.
My work is reading wording and talking to members, with **nothing hands-on**.
do: Bring the **wedding forward** and keep it small to protect the flat.
Ask about work at the **care home** where my aunt works.
Drop the **car** and eating out so Marco's wage covers rent.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake doing **sums** in my head.
S2.quote: If I lost my job, I'd be relying on my fiancé Marco, which isn't how I wanted to start a marriage.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** outright and has only three months of cushion.
She realised mid-answer that the **family books** are thinking work too, and switched to care work.
Being dependent on her **fiancé** stings against her traditional sense of partnership.

steps.text: Bring the wedding forward and hold a small church service
Ask about care assistant work at her aunt's care home
Sell the car and stop eating out
Lean on Marco's wage to cover the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, with a bit more time. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is better than two, but it's still too fast for ordinary people. At work I'd say the mutual should keep some people on the phones, because members trust a voice. I'd say it in the staff meeting, not just over tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I've got about four years left at the mutual. That's long enough to get married and maybe find a house, but not long enough for me to change into a different sort of person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the mutual and save hard, maybe 500 a month once the wedding's paid. In the second or third year I'd do a care certificate at the college, evenings, so I'm ready before 2031. We'd hold off on buying a house until we knew what my wage would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a bit sad. I'd feel like I was counting down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why say it in the staff meeting this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because with five years there's still time for them to choose. If the members are asked, I think they'd vote to keep people on the phones, and that's what being a mutual is meant to mean. I'd want it on the record that somebody asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Marco about the house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we wait. His trade is safer for longer, since the robots don't come until about 2034 here. But I don't want a mortgage we can only pay on one wage, so I'd rather rent for a few more years than lose a house.

say: I'd say five years is still **too fast** for ordinary people.
I'd tell the **staff meeting** the mutual should keep people on the phones.
think: I have about **four years** left at the mutual.
That's long enough to marry, but **not long enough** to become a different person.
do: Save about **500 a month** once the wedding is paid.
Take an evening **care certificate** in the second or third year.
**Hold off** buying a house until my wage is clear.
feel: **Anxious** and a little sad, like I'm **counting down**.
S3.quote: I don't want a mortgage we can only pay on one wage, so I'd rather rent for a few more years than lose a house.
fieldNote: Five years moves her from fear to a **countdown plan**, still reluctant.
She appeals to the mutual's **member ownership** as a reason to keep phone staff.
She delays buying a house rather than risk a **one-wage mortgage**.

steps.text: Save 500 a month once the wedding is paid off
Take an evening care certificate at the local college
Keep renting the flat above the bakery instead of buying
Raise keeping phone staff at the mutual's staff meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one, the slowest. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of warning, and people should use it. I'd still say it's sad, but I wouldn't say the sky's falling. I'd probably say we should teach young people trades again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's about the same ending for my job, just later. I'd be 37. If we've had children by then, that's the worst time to lose a wage, so I'd need to have moved before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the mutual for now, get married, and start saving for a house properly. Around year three or four, I'd take the care certificate and try part-time shifts at the care home, to see if I can do it. If it suits me, I'd switch fully before children come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious still, but steadier. I'd have time to try things without jumping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said earlier you didn't want to change into a different person. Does ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Ten years means I could do it slowly, a bit at a time, without being thrown in. Trying a few shifts isn't the same as starting over. I could still be me, just doing a different job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of your work now would you want to keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The calls where someone is frightened and you calm them down. That's the best part, and it's the same thing in a care home, really. A frightened person needs a calm voice whether their ceiling fell in or they're ninety and confused.

say: I'd say ten years is a **fair warning**, and people should use it.
I'd say we should teach young people **trades** again.
think: It's the **same ending** for my job, only later, when I'm 37.
Losing a wage once we have **children** would be the worst timing.
do: Stay at the mutual, get married and **save for a house**.
Try **part-time shifts** at the care home in year three or four.
Switch fully to care **before children** come, if it suits me.
feel: Still **anxious**, but **steadier**, with time to try things without jumping.
S4.quote: A frightened person needs a calm voice whether their ceiling fell in or they're ninety and confused.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **change slowly**, which suits her resistance to sudden change.
She links her favourite part of claims work, **calming people**, to care work.
Planned **children** shape her timeline more than AI dates do.

steps.text: Stay in household claims at the mutual for now
Start a house deposit fund after the wedding
Try part-time shifts at the care home in year three
Plan to settle into care work before having children

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. I'd have a wedding, a rented flat and three months of savings, and no job. What would help is employers paying for people to train in care or trades before they let them go, and the mutual keeping a few of us on the phones because members want that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. People at church would rally round, and that matters more to me than any scheme. I just hope we don't all need rallying at once.

headlineQuote: I don't want to train the thing that replaces me.
portrait: Elena is a 27-year-old **household claims clerk** at a member-owned mutual insurer, engaged to Marco, an electrician.
She refuses AI tools out of **distrust**, shaped by her father's job loss as a printer.
Even in AI Plateau she is uneasy, working **Saturday overtime** to pay for a wedding and rent.
Faster AGI scenarios leave her **alarmed**, and she turns to hands-on **care work** as the way out.
She leans on **family and church** before government, and wants the mutual to keep phone staff.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving her with a wedding, rent and three months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: Employers **paying for training** in care or trades before letting staff go.
The mutual keeping some **phone staff** because members want a real voice.
